paragraphs: Issi ben Akiva. (Shocher Tov, section 23; Mekhilta, Bo, section 15; Yitro, Bachodesh Hasshelishi, section 11; Mishpatim, section 4; Sifrei, beginning of Naso, at ע׳ [marker unresolved], “Every contribution for all the Israelites’ sacred gifts,” and דף כ״ז ד׳ א׳ [locators retained]. But at דף ד׳ א׳, on “The priest shall take holy water,” on “He shall abstain from wine and strong drink,” and Beha'alotekha, “Any man who is unclean through a corpse,” at כ״א ג׳, כ״ח א׳, it is ben Akavya.) Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim, chapter 8, halakhah 2: Issi ben Akavya forbids riding a mule, reasoning a fortiori from clothing, etc. They countered from Solomon’s being mounted on a mule. The answer: one does not learn from royalty, etc.; or it was a creature from the six days of creation. Tosefta, Kilayim, chapter 5, and Derekh Eretz have Issi the Babylonian forbidding riding, etc.; they countered from Solomon, and there he says, “One does not answer from Tekoa.” Cited in Tosafot, Chagigah 2b, on “to marry a maidservant”; Yalkut, Kings, section 1. See Responsa Rashba, part I, section 491, explaining this, and Rosh’s rulings on Kilayim. Pesachim 113, end of b: Rabbah bar bar Chana said in Rabbi Shmuel bar Marta’s name in Rav’s name, from Rabbi Yose (Ein Yaakov: Yosef) of Hutzal, “Whence do we know not to consult Chaldean diviners?”, etc.; “And whence,” etc. It is taught: he is Yosef of Hutzal, Yosef the Babylonian, Issi ben Gur Aryeh, Issi ben Yehudah, Issi ben Gamliel, Issi ben Mahalalel. What is his name? His name is Issi ben Akavya. (See Rav Assi.) Yoma 52, end of a: Rabbi Yochanan said, “Yosef of Hutzal asks: And the inner sanctuary within the house,” etc. Was he uncertain? Issi ben Yehudah teaches that five verses have no decisive reading, etc.; and it is taught that he is Yosef of Hutzal, Yosef the Babylonian, Issi ben Yehudah, etc.; his name is Issi ben Akiva. End quotation. Chiddushei Aggadot, Pesachim: “We do not know why he and his father had all these names. Similar names of Moses and Jethro all lend themselves to exposition.” End quotation. Responsa Halakhot Ketannot, part II, section 308: “Because of persecution they changed their fathers’ names while fleeing from place to place, to avoid recognition.” End quotation. Jerusalem Talmud, Bava Kamma, Hammanniach, halakhah 7: he is Yose the Babylonian, Yose ben Yehudah, Yose Ketanta. Why Ketanta? He was the least of the pious. End of Sotah there: because he was the essence of the righteous and pious. (See Yose and Yosef Ketanta.) He is mentioned at the end of Mishnah Sotah. See Mekhilta, Mishpatim, “You shall be holy men to Me”: Rabbi Yishmael says, “When you are holy, you are Mine”; Issi ben Yehudah says, “When the Omnipresent gives Israel a new commandment, He adds holiness to them”; Issi ben Gur Aryeh (Yalkut, Mishpatim, section 351: Gurya) says, “Holiness is stated here,” etc. This suggests Issi ben Yehudah is not Issi ben Gur Aryeh. Nedarim, chapter 11, 81a: Issi ben Yehudah did not come to Rabbi Yose’s academy for three days. Vardimos son of Rabbi Yose found him and asked, “Why has the master not come to Father’s study hall?” Rav said, “I found in Rabbi Chiyya’s secret scroll, written there: Issi ben Yehudah said,” etc.; see there. It is taught: Issi ben Yehudah enumerated the sages’ praises: “Rabbi Meir, a sage and scribe,” etc., Gittin 67a. Yuchasin, in the chronological section under Rabbi’s teachers, writes: “In Gittin, Issi ben Yehudah, a sage, and Rabbi Meir, a sage and scribe.” I think this is an error. Avot de-Rabbi Natan, end of chapter 18: Issi ben Yehudah enumerates their praises: “Rabbi Shimon learns much, forgets little.” Rabbi Shimon met him and asked, “Why do you chatter before Torah scholars?” Yuchasin also writes there, in Zevachim: Rabbi said, “When we sat before Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, Issi the Babylonian was before him, and was dear to him up to one.” (He does not remember its location; it is in the Tosefta.) See there. Menachot 18a: Rabbi said, “When I went to exhaust my measures of learning with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, I found Yosef the Babylonian sitting before him, and he was exceedingly dear to him, up to one.” Rashi: Yosef was dear to Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua; they discussed laws until reaching one law of sacrifices. Another version: everything Rabbi Elazar taught was dear to Yosef until they reached one law. Tosafot: Rav Nissim’s secret scroll reads “up to one” [עד לאחת], meaning exceedingly, since “very” is translated la-chada. Some explain: up to the soul, called yechidah. Arukh, entry chav: every answer was dear to him except one. The Mainz commentary reads “up to one” [עד אחת], without lamed. Rabbi told him, “One who slaughters,” etc.; Yosef the Babylonian’s face shone, etc.; Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua’s eyes flowed with tears: “Happy are you, Torah scholars, for words of Torah are exceedingly dear to you.” He applied to him, “How I love Your Torah; all day it is my discourse.” There too, Yosef studied with Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai (see there). Beside it is printed the above account, Tosefta, Zevachim, chapter 2, ending, “Because Rabbi Yehudah was Rabbi Ilai’s son, and Ilai was Rabbi Eliezer’s student,” etc. Thus Yuchasin there should read “in Tosefta Zevachim.” Pesachim 8b: it is taught, Issi ben Yehudah says.
